claims.claim: Your body is a friend to be cared for, not an enemy to be beaten down.
Moderation is better than going to extremes, even in holy things.

stances.summary: People who run down the body are wrong. God built it upright to look at heaven, and it becomes a dwelling for the soul and the Holy Spirit. Eat and bathe for health and strength, not for luxury.
stances.quote: Those, then, who run down created existence and vilify the body are wrong; not considering that the frame of man was formed erect for the contemplation of heaven, and that the organization of the senses tends to knowledge; and that the members and parts are arranged for good, not for pleasure.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 198-203 against teachers who despised matter. The same chapter goes on: "neither is the soul good by nature, nor, on the other hand, is the body bad by nature." Clement is no hedonist: in the Paedagogus (Book 2, ch. 1) food is for "health and strength" and plainness; in Book 3, ch. 9 the bath is for health only, never for pleasure. So his "care" is sober care. Orthodox in his own day, though never formally canonized in the West.

stances.summary: The body is not a prison to escape. It is God's own handiwork, the temple where His Spirit lives, and it will share in salvation.
stances.quote: Here he manifestly declares the body to be the temple in which the Spirit dwells.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 180 against Gnostics who despised the flesh. The point is the body's dignity and resurrection, not a rule of self-care, hence strength 1. In Book 1, ch. 28 he calls the Encratites' abstinence from animal food ingratitude "to God, who formed all things". The famous line in Book 4, ch. 20, sect. 7 ("the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God") is about the life that comes from seeing God, not about looking after the body; see misattributions.

stances.original: Etsi sufficeret illi quod nulla omnino anima salutem possit adipisci nisi dum est in carne crediderit: adeo caro salutis est cardo
stances.summary: The flesh is precious: salvation hinges on it and it will rise. But it earns its crown by suffering, through fasts, abstinence and martyrdom. Pampering it is the mark of a carnal faith.
stances.quote: It would suffice to say, indeed, that there is not a soul that can at all procure salvation, except it believe while it is in the flesh, so true is it that the flesh is the very condition on which salvation hinges.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
stances.context: Written c. 208-212, in his Montanist period (heterodox: Montanism was condemned by the wider Church). "Caro salutis cardo" (the flesh is the hinge of salvation) is the Latin. The same chapter praises the flesh because it bears "fastings, and abstinences" and martyrdom "to its own special suffering". In On Fasting, ch. 1 (Montanist, c. 210-220) he mocks the catholics: "I recognise, therefore, animal faith by its care of the flesh". So: the body is honoured as a partner, never coddled. Latin checked at thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.resurrectione.shtml.

stances.summary: Nothing God made is unclean, including the ordinary workings of the body. Only sin defiles. Yet he held up Antony, who fought bodily pleasure all his life, as the model monk.
stances.quote: Moreover if we believe man to be, as the divine Scriptures say, a work of God's hands, how could any defiled work proceed from a pure Power?
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written before 354 to calm monks who thought involuntary bodily functions made them unclean. It opens "All things made by God are beautiful and pure". In his Life of Antony (c. 357-362) Athanasius praises Antony for eating "with shame" and never bathing, and says Antony's austerity left his body sound into old age (ch. 93). Hence mixed.

stances.summary: Train the body hard and give it no soft comforts. The soul is strongest when the body's pleasures are cut back.
stances.quote: 'For,' said he, 'the fibre of the soul is then sound when the pleasures of the body are diminished.'
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Antony's words as reported by Athanasius, who knew him (Life written c. 357-362, soon after Antony died in 356). Just before: he would not anoint himself with oil, "saying it behooved young men to be earnest in training and not to seek what would enervate the body". Ch. 45: he ate and slept "with shame", yet granted "a short space to the body through its necessities". Ch. 47: he never bathed or washed his feet. Note the same Antony is the great teacher of discretion in the Sayings (see claim b). He is not an "enemy of the body" in doctrine, but his practice was stern.

stances.summary: The body is killing me, so I kill it. An old hermit who built cells in the burning heat, slept sitting up, and lived on six ounces of bread a day.
stances.quote: And once when I said to him: "What do you mean, father, at your great age by trying to kill your poor body in these heats?" he answered thus: "It kills me, I kill it."
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (SPCK), 1918
stances.context: Not in the candidate pool. Palladius lived with him c. 388 and left early, "owing to a breakdown in health", because "living with him one got parched and all dried-up". Palladius's own question shows he thought this too much. Do not confuse him with Dorotheos of Gaza (6th century).

stances.summary: A true Christian looks thin and pale from self-control; the body must be kept under. Yet medicine is God's gift, food should fit each person's needs, and refusing medical help out of piety is stubbornness.
stances.quote: the Christian is betokened by emaciation of body and paleness, which is the bloom of continence, showing that he is truly an athlete of Christ’s commandments.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK), 1925
stances.context: Written c. 360s-370s for Basil's communities. The sentence is preceded by "For as firm flesh and clear skin characterise the athlete" (the scan prints a footnote mark after "athlete"). Against this, Longer Rule 55 says medicine is God's gift: "While to avoid entirely the benefit of medicine shows a contentious spirit." Longer Rule 18 insists monks eat what is set before them to show every creature of God is good. Basil himself was chronically ill (his own letters). The 1925 translation is public domain in the US; the quote is from the OCR text of the scan, which reads cleanly here.

stances.original: θεραπευτέον, ἀδελφοί, τὸ συγγενὲς καὶ ὁμόδουλον. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ ὡς ἐχθροῦ κατηγόρησα διὰ τὸ πάθος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὡς φίλου περιέχομαι διὰ τὸν συνδήσαντα
stances.summary: My body is both friend and enemy. I accuse it as an enemy because of its passions, yet I must care for it and embrace it as a friend, because God bound us together.
stances.quote: We must care, brothers, for this kinsman and fellow slave. For even if I accused it as an enemy because of its passions, I also embrace it as a friend because of the One who bound us together.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek of PG 35, col. 868 (Migne, 1857)
stances.work: Oration 14, On Love for the Poor
stances.context: No pre-1929 English exists (NPNF 7 omits Oration 14; modern translations by Vinson and Daley are copyrighted). Greek normalized from the OCR of Migne PG 35 (archive.org scan), cols. 865-868. Section 6: "I love it as a fellow slave and turn from it as an enemy; I flee it as a chain and honour it as a co-heir" (ὃ καὶ ὡς σύνδουλον ἀγαπῶ, καὶ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ἀποστρέφομαι). Section 7: "I spare it as a fellow worker." The words are said while urging care for lepers' bodies, so "care for the body" here includes other people's bodies. Date disputed (proposals range from c. 365 to c. 380). The most exact Patristic answer to this claim: he refuses to choose.

stances.summary: Train the body so it neither runs wild from pampering nor breaks down from harsh treatment. Self-control aims at a peaceful soul, not at a tormented body.
stances.quote: The inefficiency of the body from either cause will be that which it guards against; it will train the flesh, neither making it wild and ungovernable by excessive pampering, nor sickly and unstrung and nerveless for the required work by immoderate mortification. That is temperance's highest aim; it looks not to the afflicting of the body, but to the peaceful action of the soul's functions.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Written c. 371, in praise of the celibate life, so this is an ascetic warning against over-asceticism. He compares the mind to a charioteer keeping mismatched horses together, and cites a physician on keeping the body's elements in balance.

stances.summary: Look after your health. See doctors, take the remedies, do not neglect the body out of grief or piety. Paul told Timothy to care for himself too.
stances.quote: Wherefore I beseech you dear lady, and entreat you as a very great favour to pay great attention to the restoration of your bodily health.
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9, 1889
stances.location: the letter beginning "Do not be anxious on my behalf" (second on the NPNF/New Advent page), section 1
stances.context: Written from exile in Armenia, c. 404-407, to the deaconess Olympias, ill and despondent. The same letter: "I beseech you, dear lady, to employ various and skilled physicians, and to take medicines"; section 4: "Do not then now desire death, nor neglect the means of cure ... Paul also exhorts Timothy to take the greatest care of himself." A change of mind from his youth: Palladius (Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom, ch. 5) says two years in a cave "without lying down by night or day deadened his gastric organs" and the kidneys, and ill-health drove him back to the city. Homily 1 on the Statues (387) still admires Timothy for falling "into sickness from excessive austerity", while approving Paul's correction.

stances.summary: Chastening the flesh with fasting, to bring it under the spirit, is apostolic. Those who call it madness are Epicureans.
stances.quote: So they who do not chasten their body, and desire to preach to others, are themselves esteemed reprobates.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: Letter 63, to the Church at Vercelli
stances.context: Written c. 396 against two former monks of Milan, Sarmatio and Barbatianus, who taught "that they are mad who chasten their flesh with fastings". Ambrose answers from 1 Cor 9:27 ("I chasten my body"). "Chasten" is discipline rather than hatred; Ambrose does not call the body evil. He is on the "beat it down" side against the anti-ascetics of his day.

stances.summary: There is no special merit in fasting or a frugal life. It is madness to punish the flesh with fasts.
stances.quote: for I hear that Sarmatio and Barbatianus have come to you, foolish talkers, who say that there is no merit in abstinence, no grace in a frugal life, none in virginity, that all are valued at one price, that they are mad who chasten their flesh with fastings, that they may bring it into subjection to the spirit.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: Letter 63 of Ambrose, to the Church at Vercelli
stances.context: Not in the pool. Two ex-monks of Ambrose's monastery, c. 396, followers of Jovinian's line. Known only from their opponent, who calls them Epicureans; their own words do not survive. Treat as a hostile summary. They show a real early Christian voice against bodily austerity.

stances.summary: Weaken the flesh and the soul grows strong. His own desert years were spent starving a body he called rebellious.
stances.quote: We do not expect that it will be so with us, but we look for increased vigour of soul which becomes stronger as the flesh grows weaker.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 394 to a young widow. "It" refers to Daniel's youths, whose bodies were improved by their diet; Jerome expects no such bodily gain, only a stronger soul. The same section: "Regard everything as poison which bears within it the seeds of sensual pleasure." Letter 22.7 (384) recalls his desert years: "I subdued my rebellious body with weeks of abstinence". Late letters soften the practice but not the principle: Letter 130.11 (414) still speaks of "curbing the desires of the flesh" while keeping enough strength to read and pray. See his change of mind under claim b.

stances.summary: Nobody really hates his own body. Rightly done, fasting and toil fight bad habits, not the body. Treating the body as a natural enemy is a perverse misreading of Scripture.
stances.quote: For they strive by a kind of toilsome exercise of the body itself to root out those lusts that are hurtful to the body, that is, those habits and affections of the soul that lead to the enjoyment of unworthy objects. They are not destroying themselves; they are taking care of their health.
stances.translation: James Shaw, NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written c. 396-397. The next section (25) says: "Those, on the other hand, who do this in a perverse spirit, make war upon their own body as if it were a natural enemy." He cites Eph 5:29, "No man ever yet hated his own flesh". In the Confessions (10.31.43-44, c. 397-401) he says: "I carry on a daily war by fasting, oftentimes bringing my body into subjection" and "I should bring myself to take food as medicine", but the war there is against the pleasure of eating, not the body. His Letter 211 (the rule for nuns, c. 423): "Keep the flesh under by fastings and by abstinence from meat and drink, so far as health allows."

stances.summary: Scripture forbids pampering the body, not caring for it. Feed it enough that it can do its work; cut only the craving for luxury.
stances.quote: He cuts away the luxurious fondness for the flesh: he does not exclude the control necessary for life: he does the former, lest through pampering the flesh we should be involved in dangerous entanglements of the desires; the latter lest the body should be injured by our fault and unable to fulfil its spiritual and necessary duties.
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 420-424. "He" is Paul in Rom 13:14 ("take not care for the flesh in its lusts"). Cassian is still an ascetic: the same book says "Perfection of mind indeed depends upon the abstinence of the belly" (5.9), and his diet is strict by modern standards. Strength 1 because the care he allows is minimal.

stances.original: Nos non edocti sumus corporis interfectores esse, sed affectuum. (Latin of PG 65, Poemen 184; Greek: οὐκ ἐδιδάχθημεν σωματοκτόνοι, ἀλλὰ παθοκτόνοι)
stances.summary: We were taught to kill our passions, not our bodies. Caught washing his feet by a monk who admired the harsh old fathers, he defended looking after the body.
stances.quote: We have not learned to be slayers of the body, but slayers of the passions.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Book of Paradise)
stances.location: vol. 2, Book 2, chapter 1 (Questions and Answers), saying 166, pp. 189-190
stances.context: Abba Isaac saw him "pouring some water over his feet" and asked how, when the fathers "oppressed their bodies", he could wash his feet. Poemen (Egypt, 5th century) is known only through the Sayings, collected in the 5th-6th centuries. In the alphabetical collection this is Poemen 184 (checked in the Latin and Greek of PG 65). Budge's printing puts a quotation mark at the start of every continued line, so the scan text reads "... of the body, / " but slayers ...".

stances.original: per quod multi dum nimio fervore mentis rationem suarum virium non haberent, subito conciderunt, et pene ante debilitatem, quam sanctitatem de proposito suo consecuti sunt. Optimus est in omni re modus, et laudabilis ubique mensura. Corpus non frangendum, sed regendum est.
stances.summary: Do not break the body; govern it. Many zealous people ignored their limits, collapsed, and got weakness instead of holiness.
stances.quote: Many, in too much fervour of mind, took no account of their strength and suddenly collapsed, reaching weakness almost before holiness. In everything measure is best, and moderation is praiseworthy everywhere. The body is not to be broken, but ruled.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin of PL 30 (Migne), printed among the works of Jerome
stances.context: Written 413 to the young Roman noblewoman Demetrias on taking the veil. Heterodox: Pelagius was condemned in 416-418. The letter survived under Jerome's name (PL 30, "Mantissa" to Jerome), so its lines are sometimes quoted as Jerome's. The only English (B. R. Rees, 1991) is copyrighted. Latin normalized from the OCR of the Migne scan (e.g. "proposilo" read as "proposito", "frangendum" confirmed). Pelagius still commends fasting in the same chapter; the target is excess.

stances.summary: A body that loves comfort cannot hold the knowledge of God. The body is sin's ally and must be pressed down, even near to death.
stances.quote: The knowledge of God does not dwell in a body that loves comfort.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam), 1923
stances.work: Ascetical Homilies (Wensinck: Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence)
stances.context: Isaac, bishop of Nineveh in the late 7th century, belonged to the Church of the East (outside the Chalcedonian churches), yet is venerated as a saint by the Orthodox. The next line: "A man who loves his body will not be deemed worthy of divine gifts." Treatise XXXV (pp. 179-180) goes further: the body pleads "Leave me a while to behave with moderation", and the monk is told not to believe it; but that passage opens "For one of the saints says", so where Isaac's quotation ends is unclear. He also writes (opening of Treatise I): "I do not call separation the departure from the body, but from the bodily things." The scan title page OCR reads "1933"; the book is Verhandelingen KAW, Nieuwe Reeks XXIII no. 1, 1923.

stances.original: Quomodo oderim quem natura diligo? ... Idem enim et hostis est et adjutor, auxiliator et adversarius, opitulator et insidiator. Cum bene curatur et fovetur, insolescit et insultat; maceratus deficit ... Si frangam, per quem virtutes exerceam non habeo: eumdem aversor et amplector.
stances.summary: The body is my friend and my enemy at once. Cherish it and it grows unruly; break it and I have nothing to practise virtue with. I turn from it and embrace it.
stances.quote: How can I hate what by nature I love? He is at once my enemy and my helper, my ally and my adversary, my support and my ambusher. Cared for and cherished, he grows insolent; worn down, he fails. If I break him, I have nothing with which to practise the virtues. I turn from him and I embrace him.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin version (Rader) printed with the Greek in PG 88, cols. 901-904 (Migne, 1860)
stances.context: Written at Sinai in the first half of the 7th century. The Greek columns of this scan are badly garbled, so the rendering follows the facing Latin translation (itself made from the Greek); check against a Greek edition before printing. No pre-1929 English was found (Moore 1959 and Luibheid-Russell 1982 are copyrighted). The same passage asks: "how am I to myself both enemy and friend?" (quomodo mihi ipse hostis et amicus sum). The body then answers that it cannot be tamed except by humility.

stances.original: Balnearum usus infirmis, quoties expedit, offeratur. Sanis autem, et maxime juvenibus, tardius concedatur.
stances.summary: Chastise the body and avoid soft living, but the sick come before everything: give them baths, meat and care, and hold the healthy young to more austerity.
stances.quote: Let the use of baths be allowed to the sick as often as may be expedient ; but to those who are well, and especially to the young, let it be granted more seldom.
stances.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed., Fort Augustus 1906 (archive.org scan catalogued 1907)
stances.context: Written c. 530-560. Chapter 36 opens "Before all things and above all things care is to be had of the sick". Chapter 4 lists among the tools of good works "11. To chastise the body. 12. Not to seek after delicate living." Gregory the Great (Dialogues 2.2) says the young Benedict once threw himself naked into nettles and briars to master temptation, "so by the wounds of his body, he cured the wounds of his soul"; the Rule he wrote later is far gentler. The scan prints a space before semicolons.

stances.summary: A Christian should die on sackcloth and ashes, not on a soft bed. Even in a fever he made his worn-out limbs serve his spirit.
stances.quote: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Letter 3 of Sulpicius Severus, to Bassula
stances.context: Martin's words on his deathbed (397), reported by Sulpicius Severus, who knew him well and wrote the same year. His disciples begged him to allow "some common straw". This is penitential humility at death as much as a view of the body; strength 1. Sulpicius says he "compelled his worn-out limbs to do service to his spirit".

stances.original: Ἐὰν ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον τείνω, κλᾶται τὸ τόξον. Λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ γέρων· Οὕτως καὶ εἰς τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ· ἐὰν πλεῖον τοῦ μέτρου τείνωμεν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ταχὺ προσρήσσουσι. Χρὴ οὖν μίαν μίαν συγκαταβαίνειν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.
stances.summary: Even in the work of God, a bow bent too far snaps. People who wear their bodies out without discernment end up far from God.
stances.quote: "Put an arrow to your bow and draw it." He did so. "Draw again," he said, and he drew. And again, "Draw." The hunter said, "If I draw it beyond measure, the bow will break." The old man said, "So it is in the work of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they soon break. So now and then we must come down to the brothers' level."
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (with Cotelier's Latin) of PG 65, Apophthegmata Patrum, Antony 13 (cols. 77-80)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (alphabetical collection)
stances.context: A hunter was shocked to see Antony relaxing and joking with the brothers. The Sayings were collected in the 5th-6th centuries, long after Antony (d. 356). Greek normalized from OCR of the Migne scan. Also in the Sayings, a public-domain English line: "Many have afflicted themselves with labours and tribulations, and because they had not in them the power of discernment, they did not know the way of truth" (Budge, Paradise vol. 2, 1907, p. 283, quoted by Anan-Isho; the OCR reads "ot" for "of"). Latin Verba Seniorum 5.10.1: "Quia sunt quidam conterentes corpora sua in abstinentia; sed quia non habuerunt discretionem, longe facti sunt a Deo." Cassian (Conferences 2.2, NPNF 11) has Antony teach that discretion "passing by excess on either side, teaches a monk always to walk along the royal road". His own practice was severe (see claim a).

stances.original: Ἔστι καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ ἐπιτεταμένη ἄσκησις· καὶ γὰρ οἱ αὐτοῦ μαθηταὶ τοῦτο ποιοῦσι. Πῶς οὖν διακρίνωμεν τὴν θείαν καὶ βασιλικὴν ἄσκησιν τῆς τυραννικῆς καὶ δαιμονιώδους; Δῆλον ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς συμμετρίας. Ἅπας σοι ὁ χρόνος εἷς κανὼν νηστείας ὑπαρχέτω. Μὴ τέσσαρας ἢ πέντε νηστεύσῃς, καὶ τὴν ἄλλην ἐν πλήθει τροφῶν καταλύσῃς· πανταχοῦ γὰρ ἡ ἀμετρία φθοροποιὸς τυγχάνει.
stances.summary: Extreme asceticism can come from the devil, whose followers also fast. Real, God-given discipline is known by its balance: keep one steady rule rather than binge-fasting and then feasting.
stances.quote: There is also an intense asceticism that comes from the enemy, for his disciples practise it too. How then shall we tell the divine and royal asceticism from the tyrannical and demonic kind? Plainly, by its balance. Let one rule of fasting hold for all your time. Do not fast four or five days and then break the fast the next day with a mass of food. For everywhere, lack of measure is destructive.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek of PG 65, Apophthegmata Patrum, Syncletica 15 (cols. 425-428)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (alphabetical collection)
stances.context: Syncletica (Egypt, 4th-5th century) is known through the Sayings and a Life falsely ascribed to Athanasius. No public-domain English was found (Ward 1975 is copyrighted). Greek normalized from the OCR of the Migne scan; the facing Latin reads "Manifestum est quod ex mediocritate ... Ubique immoderatio exitiosa est." She adds: "While you are young and healthy, fast, for old age will come with weakness." Her balance is still strict: steady daily fasting, not ease.

stances.summary: Eat a little every day rather than fasting for days on end. He did the long fasts when young, but the old men tested them all and found the small daily meal was the better road.
stances.quote: the old men, like men of might, have tried all these by experience, but they have found that it is beneficial for a man to eat an exceedingly small quantity of food each day, and because of this they have delivered unto us an easy way to the kingdom.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Book of Paradise)
stances.location: vol. 2, Book 1, chapter 2 (Of Fasting and Abstinence), saying 102, pp. 22-23
stances.context: Abba Joseph asked him how to fast. Poemen: "I prefer the man who eateth every day a very small quantity of food, and who doth not satisfy his cravings for food." Joseph: "When thou wast a young man didst thou not fast two days at a time?" Poemen: "Yea, I did, and three days at a time, and four days at a time, and even a week at a time". A personal change of mind from youth to age. In the alphabetical collection this is Poemen 31; the Latin of PG 65 ends "atque nobis tradiderunt viam quae regia est, quia levis" (and they handed down to us the road that is royal, because it is light). Budge's line-initial quotation marks are OCR'd as "1", "'" or "*" in the scan text.

stances.summary: A small, steady daily meal is better than long harsh fasts followed by relaxing. Excessive fasting wrecks both the mind and prayer.
stances.quote: A reasonable supply of food partaken of daily with moderation, is better than a severe and long fast at intervals. Excessive fasting has been known not only to undermine the constancy of the mind, but also to weaken the power of prayers through sheer weariness of body.
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 420-424 for monks in Gaul, from what he learned in Egypt. Book 5, ch. 5: "on the manner of fasting a uniform rule cannot easily be observed, because everybody has not the same strength". Ch. 24: Egyptian elders broke their fasts to feed guests, since "a fast, although it is useful and advisable, is yet a free-will offering" while charity is a command. His "moderation" is still one small meal a day.

stances.summary: Extremes meet: too much fasting and gluttony end in the same place. Discretion walks between them, and excess of abstinence is even more dangerous than careless eating.
stances.quote: We ought then with all our might to strive for the virtue of discretion by the power of humility, as it will keep us uninjured by either extreme, for there is an old saying ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες, i.e., extremes meet. For excess of fasting and gluttony come to the same thing
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Cassian puts these words in the mouth of Abba Moses of Scetis, whom he met c. 385-399, and wrote them up c. 425-429, so the wording is Cassian's. Moses is often identified with Moses the Black (the Ethiopian), but this is not certain: Cassian (Conference 3.5) separately mentions an "Abbot Moses, who lived in a spot in the wilderness called Calamus" who fled to a monastery after a murder. If the identification holds, this is Moses the Black's later view, after the extremes recorded by Palladius (see his stance). In ch. 17 Moses recalls his own over-fasting and sleeplessness and concludes: "excessive abstinence is still more injurious to us than careless satiety".

stances.summary: Tormented by temptation, he kept going to extremes: tiny rations, standing awake for six years, carrying water by night. Told to stop, he refused to cease until the demons ceased.
stances.quote: So the great Isidore said to him: "Moses, stop struggling with the demons, and do not provoke them." But he said to him: "I will never cease until the appearance of the demons ceases."
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (SPCK), 1918
stances.context: Palladius (in Egypt c. 388-399; wrote c. 419-420) records this of Moses the Ethiopian, a former robber. After a demon's blow left him ill "for a year", Isidore declared his dreams ended and told him the struggle was allowed "that you should not boast of having overcome passion". So the story itself shows the limits of extremes. Only this one sentence is Moses's own recorded word on the matter; hence strength 1. For a possible later, moderate Moses, see "Abba Moses (Cassian)".

stances.summary: One hour of sleep is enough for a monk who fights. He kept all-night vigils and called sleep a wicked servant girl.
stances.quote: One hour's sleep is sufficient for a monk, provided that he be strenuous.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Book of Paradise)
stances.location: vol. 2, Book 1, chapter 3 (Of the Reading of the Scriptures, and of Watching by Night...), saying 134, pp. 29-30
stances.context: Arsenius (c. 350-445), once a tutor at the imperial court, lived at Scetis. Saying 133, from his disciple Daniel: he would pass the night in vigil and say to sleep, "Get thee gone, O wicked handmaiden". The scan OCRs Budge's opening quotation marks as "44" and breaks "suffi-cient" across a line. Balance: another saying (Budge vol. 2, no. 450) has a priest defend giving the sick Arsenius a mat and pillow, since he had left a palace for this; and in the Latin Verba Seniorum 5.10.7 (PL 73), when Abba Mark praises a brother who pulled up the few vegetables in his cell, Arsenius answers: "Bonum quidem est, sed secundum exercitationem hominis uniuscujusque agendum est" (it is good, but each must act according to his own state of training).

stances.summary: He lived for years on bread and oil, with no fruit, vegetables, meat or baths. Yet he taught that a dry but even diet joined to love, not wild swings, leads to peace of soul.
stances.quote: From the time that I took to the desert, I have not touched lettuce nor any other green vegetable, nor any fruit, nor grapes, nor meat, nor a bath.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (SPCK), 1918
stances.context: Evagrius (d. 399) told this to Palladius, his disciple. Heterodox: condemned with Origenism at Constantinople in 553. LH 38.13: in his sixteenth year without cooked food "his flesh felt a need, owing to the weakness of the stomach" and he changed his diet. His teaching, preserved in Latin as Verba Seniorum 5.1.4 (PL 73): "quod siccior et non inaequalis victus charitati conjunctus, citius introducat monachum in portum impassibilitatis" (a rather dry and even diet, joined to love, brings the monk more quickly into the harbour of dispassion); in Greek this is Praktikos 91 (not checked in Greek here). The Historia Monachorum (Budge vol. 1) says he told visitors not to drink their fill of water.

stances.summary: The true and elect do not give up their fast even when starving, emaciated and half blind. Giving way at hunger or slight illness is the mark of the shaky.
stances.quote: The true and elect, however, do not even satisfy their hunger with herbs and vegetables. But, feeding upon drugs and dry stubble, even then they are not to be persuaded to open their mouth for food, before the fixed time.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam), 1923
stances.work: Ascetical Homilies (Wensinck: On the various ways in which Satan fights)
stances.context: Late 7th century; Church of the East. The sentence continues: "Lying on the earth, with an emaciated body and eyes blinded on account of bodily weakness ... even then they do not give way" (Wensinck notes that Isaac himself is said to have gone blind). Balance: Treatise XV (pp. 138-139) lets a weak monk drop the psalms and prostrations, but still says "But do not sleep". Treatise XXXV has the body plead "Leave me a while to behave with moderation", which the monk must refuse (voice uncertain, see claim a).

stances.original: Vltro cibum, quibus modis quibusque temporibus potuissem, pro ueneno deputarem et antidotum famem sumerem, per quam purgarem mortis a primordio causam
stances.summary: Fast more, not less. Adam fell by eating, so treat food as poison and hunger as the antidote. The mainstream Church's moderation in fasting is gluttony dressed up.
stances.quote: Unbidden, I would, in such ways and at such times as I might have been able, have habitually accounted food as poison, and taken the antidote, hunger; through which to purge the primordial cause of death
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Montanist period, c. 210-220 (heterodox). A whole treatise defending the Montanists' extra fasts, late fasts and "xerophagies" (dry diet) against the catholics, whom he calls "Psychics" (the unspiritual). Ch. 2 reports the catholic view he attacks: fasting "to be indifferently observed ... of choice, not of command, according to the times and needs of each individual". Latin checked at thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.ieiunio.shtml.

stances.summary: In all things the middle course is good and the extremes are dangerous. Eat simply and enough, neither greedily nor in fear of God's good gifts.
stances.quote: In all things, indeed, this is the case, and not least in the preparation made for feasting, since the extremes are dangerous, and middle courses good.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 190-200. The immediate subject is meals ("our meals are to be taken with love; and in these the medium state is good"), so its application to "holy things" is Clement's general rule rather than a teaching on fasting; strength 1. He goes on: "to be in no want of necessaries is the medium. For the desires which are in accordance with nature are bounded by sufficiency."

stances.summary: Ascetic extremism that forbids marriage and meat is not holiness. It insults the Creator who made these things good.
stances.quote: Some of those reckoned among them have also introduced abstinence from animal food, thus proving themselves ungrateful to God, who formed all things.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 180 about the Encratites ("self-controlled"), led by Tatian, who "preached against marriage". His objection is doctrinal (they deny the goodness of creation), not a general rule of moderation; strength 1.

stances.summary: Ascetics who abstain from meat and wine and forbid marriage to magnify themselves are puffed up with pride. They are more like Cynic philosophers than Christians.
stances.quote: In respect, however, of their mode of life, they pass their days inflated with pride. They suppose, that by meats they magnify themselves, while abstaining from animal food, (and) being water-drinkers, and forbidding to marry, and devoting themselves during the remainder of life to habits of asceticism. But persons of this description are estimated Cynics rather than Christians
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Book 8, chapter 13 (ANF numbering; 8.20 in modern editions)
stances.context: Written c. 225-235. The attribution of the Refutation to Hippolytus is traditional but disputed by some scholars. The Encratites here "acknowledge some things concerning God and Christ in like manner with the Church"; the charge is pride and extremism of life. He cites 1 Tim 4:1-5.

stances.summary: The golden mean is the wrong test. What matters is where a feeling is aimed, not how strong it is: an ardent love of the right thing is no fault, and even a moderate love of the wrong thing is a great vice.
stances.quote: We must not, they say, rejoice with excessive joy, but moderately and temperately. This is as though they should say that we must not run swiftly, but walk quietly. But it is possible that he who walks may err, and that he who runs may keep the right path.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written c. 303-311, against the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) doctrine that the passions should be kept to a mean. The same chapter: "What then, I pray, will this mediocrity profit us?" and "sensual desire, if it does not wander from its lawful object, although it be ardent, yet is without fault. But if it desires an unlawful object, although it be moderate, yet it is a great vice." His subject is emotions, not fasting, so he is a principled voice against moderation as the rule, not an advocate of extreme austerity. In 6.15 he also rejects the Stoic extreme of cutting the passions out.

stances.summary: There is no one rule of food for everyone. Needs differ by age, work and constitution, and superiors must adjust for the sick and the weary. Avoid both extremes.
stances.quote: But as regards food, different men have different needs, which vary according to age and occupation and proportionately to the habit of the body ; so also is the measure and fashion of the use of food.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK), 1925
stances.context: Longer Rule 18: monks should eat all that is set before them, so as to "free ourselves from the suspicion of falling into either extreme", voluptuaries on one side and Manichean food-haters on the other. Longer Rule 19 continues: "it is incongruous to take food in order to sustain the body and then by means of this very food to wage war with the body". Strength 1 because Basil also praises emaciation (claim a) and his measure is very strict. The scan prints a space before the semicolon.

stances.summary: Some fall into the opposite excess: so busy tormenting the body that they can no longer lift their minds to God. Guard against both errors.
stances.quote: Many, however, slide into the very opposite kind of excess, and unconsciously to themselves, in their over-preciseness, laboriously thwart their own design
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: c. 371. The sentence continues: their minds are "so bent upon regulations which merely affect the body, that they can no longer walk in their heavenly freedom and gaze above; their only inclination is to this tormenting and afflicting of the flesh." Then: "let every one remember that wise precept, which warns us from turning to the right hand or to the left."

stances.summary: In a good community no one is pushed beyond his strength. Those who refuse wine or meat they need for their health are being superstitious, not holy.
stances.quote: Many drink no wine; but they do not think that wine defiles them; for they cause it to be given with the greatest propriety and moderation to people of languid temperament, and, in short, to all who cannot have bodily health without it. When some foolishly refuse it, they counsel them as brothers not to let a silly superstition make them weaker instead of making them holier.
stances.translation: Richard Stothert, NPNF 1st series vol. 4, 1887
stances.work: On the Morals of the Catholic Church
stances.context: Written 388, describing communities he saw in Milan and Rome, against the Manichees. Section 71: "no one is pressed to endure hardships for which he is unfit; nothing is imposed on any one against his will; nor is he condemned by the rest because he confesses himself too feeble to imitate them". But section 70 admires those who fasted "three days or more in succession without food or drink" as long as it was voluntary. Letter 211 (c. 423): fast "so far as health allows".

stances.summary: Early Jerome: in the desert he starved his body for weeks, and years later he only regretted that he could no longer keep up that pace.
stances.quote: Helpless, I cast myself at the feet of Jesus, I watered them with my tears, I wiped them with my hair: and then I subdued my rebellious body with weeks of abstinence. I do not blush to avow my abject misery; rather I lament that I am not now what once I was.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 384 about his desert years (c. 375-377). Even this letter gives moderate daily advice (22.17: "Take food in moderation ... It is idle to carry an empty stomach if, in two or three days' time, the fast is to be made up for by repletion"), while wanting companions "pale and thin with fasting". Later in 384 his young disciple Blesilla died after severe fasting and Rome blamed him (Letters 38-39). Earlier view; see his later stance.

stances.summary: Later Jerome: no extreme fasting. Virtue is a mean, "nothing too much". Keep enough strength to read, sing and keep vigil.
stances.quote: I do not, however, lay on you as an obligation any extreme fasting or abnormal abstinence from food. Such practices soon break down weak constitutions and cause bodily sickness before they lay the foundations of a holy life. It is a maxim of the philosophers that virtues are means, and that all extremes are of the nature of vice
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written 414, the same year and to the same young woman as Pelagius's letter (see Pelagius). He goes on: "You must not go on fasting until your heart begins to throb and your breath to fail". Letter 107.10 (to Laeta, c. 403): "I strongly disapprove — especially for those of tender years — of long and immoderate fasts ... I have learned by experience". Letter 130.17 and 125.16 describe hermits made mad by "excessive fasting". The change of mind is real, but the principle that the flesh must be curbed stays (claim a).

stances.summary: Guard against lack of measure on either side: look after the body's health and trim its luxury. Paul told the over-fasting Timothy to drink a little wine.
stances.quote: Let us guard then against a want of moderation on either side, and let us take care of the health of the body, at the same time that we prune away its luxurious propensities.
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Preached at Antioch in 387 on 1 Tim 5:23. Strength 1 because the homily also praises Timothy's "divine wisdom and strictness" in falling "into sickness from excessive austerity" (sect. 8), and reads Paul's "a little wine" as "a recommendation of abstinence". Chrysostom had ruined his own health in the desert (Palladius, Dialogue 5).

stances.summary: Fasting or eating is not the point; reason and faith are. Wine taken with good sense is holier than water drunk with pride.
stances.quote: For to drink wine with reason is better than to drink water with pride. And, please, look on those who drink wine with reason as holy men and those who drink water without reason as profane men
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (SPCK), 1918
stances.context: Not in the pool, but the chief historian of the Egyptian monks (wrote c. 419-420; disciple of Evagrius, later bishop and defender of Chrysostom). Same passage: "For if you partake reasonably and abstain reasonably you will never sin" and "neither is eating nor refraining anything, but faith extending itself in love to works". He also asked Dorotheus why he was killing his body (see Dorotheus).

stances.summary: Fasting earns no more merit than eating with thanksgiving. Virgins and married, fasters and eaters, stand equal before God.
stances.quote: His third point is that there is no difference between abstinence from food, and its reception with thanksgiving.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Not in the pool. A Roman monk condemned c. 390-393 by Pope Siricius and by a synod under Ambrose. His books are lost; this is Jerome's hostile summary (393), which quotes Jovinian elsewhere at length. He goes further than "moderation": he denies fasting any special merit. Jerome's Book 2 is the reply on fasting.

stances.original: Generaliter quidem, sed breviter strictimque dicendum est: in bonis quoque rebus quidquid modum excesserit, vitium est.
stances.summary: Even good things become faults when pushed past measure. Immoderate fasts and wild vigils are just intemperance in a holy costume.
stances.quote: It must be said generally, but briefly and strictly: even in good things, whatever goes beyond measure is a fault.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin of PL 30 (Migne), printed among the works of Jerome
stances.context: Written 413; heterodox (condemned 416-418). Chapter 23 just before: "immoderata jejunia et ardor abstinentiae, et enormes inordinataeque vigiliae, intemperantiae coarguuntur" (immoderate fasts, burning zeal for abstinence, and huge disordered vigils stand convicted of intemperance). The closest early Christian statement of the claim word for word. Latin normalized from the OCR ("XXTY" read as XXIV).

stances.original: Haec ergo aliaque testimonia discretionis matris virtutum sumens, sic omnia temperet, ut et sit quod fortes cupiant, et infirmi non refugiant.
stances.summary: Discretion is the mother of virtues. The abbot must set the measure so the strong have something to aim at and the weak are not frightened away.
stances.quote: Taking, then, the testimonies borne by these and the like words to discretion, the mother of virtues, let him so temper all things, that the strong may have something to strive after, and the weak nothing at which to take alarm.
stances.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 2nd ed., Fort Augustus 1906 (archive.org scan catalogued 1907)
stances.context: c. 530-560. Same chapter: the abbot must not "scrape off the rust" so hard that "the vessel be broken". Prologue: "we hope to order nothing that is harsh or rigorous". Chapter 40 allows a pint (hemina) of wine a day, "although we read that wine ought by no means to be the drink of monks". Gregory the Great (Dialogues 2.36, 593-594) says Benedict "wrote a rule for his monks, both excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style" (discretione praecipuam).

stances.summary: The abstinent are in danger too: when the flesh is worn down more than it needs, a show of humility hides great pride inside.
stances.quote: Here it is to be noted that the excellent preacher, in his argument, joins a show of humility to superstition, because, when the flesh is worn more than needs by abstinence, humility is displayed outwardly, but on account of this very humility there is grievous pride within.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written 590-591. The chapter treats gluttons and the abstinent evenhandedly: "In vain, then, is the body worn by abstinence, if the mind, abandoned to disorderly emotions, is dissipated by vices", and the abstinent must give the poor what they deny themselves. Strength 1: he warns about excess rather than making moderation his theme. Personally he valued the fast highly: in Dialogues 3.33 he tells how, so ill he had to eat constantly, he grieved more at missing the Holy Saturday fast than at his sickness, and prayed to be able to fast.

stances.summary: Simeon took on every extreme he heard of: immoderate fasting, standing day and night, and finally decades on a pillar. His abbot had to force him to loosen a rope he had bound into his flesh.
stances.quote: And when he learned from many about their courses of life, he began to adopt them for himself, immoderate fasting, standing day and night, continual prayer, persistent supplication, godly zeal which burned like a fire in him, bodily chastity with purity of his members.
stances.translation: Frederick Lent, "The Life of Simeon Stylites", Journal of the American Oriental Society 35, 1915
stances.context: Not in the pool. The Syriac Life was written c. 473 by disciples, about 14 years after his death (459). These are the biographers' words about his practice, not Simeon's own words, so strength 1. The Life says he "gave no enjoyment to his body even for one hour" and lost his sight for forty days "from fasting and vigil beyond measure". Evagrius Scholasticus (Church History 1.13, c. 593; Walford 1846) reports that the desert fathers, suspicious of this "strange and hitherto unknown walk", ordered him down to test his obedience. Theodoret's Religious History 26, an eyewitness account defending the novelty, was not checked in the original here.

stances.summary: The young Origen went to every extreme: bare feet, no bed, almost no food or wine, and self-castration in a literal reading of Matthew 19:12.
stances.quote: He is said to have walked for a number of years never wearing a shoe, and, for a great many years, to have abstained from the use of wine, and of all other things beyond his necessary food; so that he was in danger of breaking down and destroying his constitution.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.context: Eusebius (writing c. 311-325, using Origen's letters and people who knew him) reports Origen's practice c. 203-210; these are not Origen's words, so strength 1. Book 6, ch. 8 calls the castration "an immature and youthful mind" taking the verse "in too literal and extreme a sense". Heterodox: Origen was condemned posthumously in 553. Lead not checked here: Origen's own Commentary on Matthew, Book 15 (Greek; no public-domain English, ANF 9 omits it) argues against a literal reading of Matt 19:12, which would be a later change of mind.

splits_fathers: Claim a: very few early Christians gave a clean yes or no. The common view is "both": the body is God's good work, a temple and a partner in salvation, and it must also be disciplined. Clear care-for-it voices: Clement, Augustine (On Christian Doctrine), Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom (late), Cassian, Poemen, Pelagius. Clear beat-it-down voices: Dorotheus ("It kills me, I kill it"), Jerome, Isaac the Syrian, Ambrose (against the anti-ascetics), Antony (practice), Martin (deathbed). Deliberate "both": Gregory of Nazianzus ("as an enemy ... as a friend"), John Climacus ("my enemy and my helper"), Basil, Tertullian, Benedict, Athanasius. The only people who plainly denied the value of bodily austerity (Jovinian, Sarmatio and Barbatianus) were condemned. Claim b: a large majority of the teachers argued for measure and discretion, often bluntly (Antony's bow, Syncletica, Poemen, Cassian and Abba Moses, Nyssa, Augustine, later Jerome, Pelagius, Benedict, Basil, Palladius). But real voices sit on the other side: Tertullian's On Fasting, Isaac the Syrian, Arsenius, the young Moses the Black, the young Jerome, Simeon Stylites, the young Origen, and Lactantius in principle. Several people changed sides with age (Jerome, Poemen, Chrysostom; possibly Moses). Key caveat: their "moderation" is steady daily austerity (one small meal, no meat, little sleep), not modern moderation. Their reason for it is usually that extremes breed pride and collapse, not that the body deserves comfort.
splits_people_today: Claim a is one-sided today. Almost everyone, Christian or not, would agree that the body should be cared for (wellness culture, "your body is a temple", body positivity). Only a minority would hesitate: traditional Catholics and Orthodox who practise mortification and strict Lenten fasting, some very disciplined athletes, and people shaped by purity culture or shame about the body. As worded, it will barely separate players, and it misses the Fathers' real tension. A sharper statement would split people more, e.g. "A bit of hunger and discomfort now and then is good for your soul" or "The more you give your body what it wants, the weaker your will gets." Claim b splits more than it looks. Most people will say yes to moderation in general. But many committed Christians distrust moderation in faith: "lukewarm" (Rev 3:16), "radical discipleship", "all in for Jesus", total fasts, and among secular people the "no half measures", extreme-discipline culture. Framing it around devotion ("You can pray, fast or give too much") would split believers roughly down the middle.

misattributions.line: The glory of God is man fully alive.
misattributions.truth: A loose modern paraphrase, often used to mean self-fulfilment or taking care of yourself. Against Heresies 4.20.7 (ANF 1) reads: "For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God." The point is that true life comes from seeing God, not a teaching on body care.

misattributions.line: The body is not to be broken but governed. / In everything measure is best. / Even in good things, whatever goes beyond measure is a fault.
misattributions.truth: From Pelagius, Letter to Demetrias (413), ch. 21 and 24. The letter was transmitted among Jerome's works and Migne still prints it in PL 30 in the appendix to Jerome ("Hieronymi operum mantissa"), so these lines can surface under Jerome's name. Jerome's own letter to the same Demetrias (Letter 130, 414) says something similar in other words.

misattributions.line: Take care of your body as if you were going to live forever; take care of your soul as if you were going to die tomorrow.
misattributions.truth: A widely circulated internet attribution. It was not found in the Augustine texts read here, and no source for it is known to me; treat it as unsourced. A similar thought ("live as if you will die tomorrow, but treat the body as if you will live with it many years") is credited to Macarius by Evagrius, Praktikos 29, from memory; that was not checked in the original this session.

notes: Totals: claim a has 21 stances (9 agree, 6 mixed, 6 disagree); claim b has 27 (18 agree, 8 disagree, 1 mixed), counting Jerome twice for his change of mind. Own renderings (no public-domain English found): Gregory of Nazianzus (Or. 14), John Climacus (Step 15, from the Latin version), Antony (bow saying) and Syncletica 15 (Greek of PG 65), and Pelagius (Latin of PL 30). Their Greek or Latin was read in the OCR of Migne scans on archive.org and normalized by hand, so check against a modern critical text before printing. Budge 1907, Wensinck 1923, Clarke 1918 and 1925, and Hunter Blair 1906 are public domain; their archive.org texts are OCR. The quotes above are spelled as printed, but the raw scan text has stray quotation marks at line starts and hyphenated line breaks, so any machine check of those five sources must normalize whitespace, hyphens and line-initial quote marks. Not found or not usable for this topic: Ignatius, Justin, Perpetua, Cyprian, Novatian (On Jewish Meats praises moderation of appetite against luxury, but not against ascetic extremes), Hilary, Ephrem, Paulinus of Nola, Boethius, Macrina. Macrina: Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina (Clarke 1916) says she refused a doctor for a tumour because she "judged it worse than the pain, to uncover any part of the body to a stranger's eyes", and died lying on a sack on boards. That is modesty and poverty, and a report rather than her own words, so no stance was recorded. Moses the Black: the only words of his own are LH 19.10; the moderate "Abba Moses" of Cassian may or may not be the same man, so he is kept as a separate entry. Evagrius Scholasticus, Theodoret on Simeon, and Origen's Commentary on Matthew 15 are leads not verified in the original. For the reveal, the most vivid lines are: Dorotheus "It kills me, I kill it"; Poemen "slayers of the passions"; Gregory of Nazianzus "as an enemy ... as a friend"; Antony's bow; Syncletica's "demonic asceticism"; Isaac's starving elect; Tertullian's "food as poison"; Pelagius "even in good things, whatever goes beyond measure is a fault"; Jerome's before-and-after. Players who choose moderation on b will match almost everyone, since most early teachers held it. To make b discriminate, pair it with a statement about intensity in devotion, where Isaac, Tertullian, Arsenius and the young Jerome stand out. Web search was unavailable (the session budget was spent), so sources were found through known archives (New Advent, tertullian.org, archive.org) and read in raw text.
